cls: Intravenous electrolyte / systemic alkalinizing agent (lactate-to-bicarbonate source)
quick: Individualized IV infusion based on acid-base/fluid status (e.g., compound sodium lactate/Hartmann's by need)
Compound sodium lactate widely used; acceptable when indicated
Caution - risk of fluid overload, hyperkalemia, and impaired lactate clearance
Caution / avoid in severe hepatic impairment (cannot convert lactate to bicarbonate)
Not relevant in acute IV use
Electrolytes, acid-base status, fluid balance, blood pressure
summary: Sodium lactate is a parenteral source of sodium and lactate; the lactate is metabolized in the liver to bicarbonate, providing systemic alkalinization and treating metabolic acidosis. It is the alkalinizing component of balanced crystalloids such as compound sodium lactate (Hartmann's/lactated Ringer's). Molar/hypertonic sodium lactate is also used to correct metabolic acidosis and as a sodium source. Dosing is individualized to fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base needs, with caution in renal failure, heart failure, and severe hepatic impairment. (EMA/SmPC/BNF product, not a single US FDA oral monograph.)
indications: Source of bicarbonate (via lactate metabolism) for treatment of metabolic acidosis
Fluid and electrolyte replacement as the alkalinizing component of balanced crystalloids (compound sodium lactate / Hartmann's solution)
Sodium replacement / volume expansion when an alkalinizing electrolyte solution is required

dosage.d: Individualized IV dose calculated from base deficit and clinical status
dosage.n: Adjust to acid-base response; avoid over-correction

dosage.d: Volume titrated to fluid and electrolyte needs (e.g., 500-1000 mL infusions)
dosage.n: Contains Na, K, Ca, Cl, and lactate; rate per clinical need

dosage.d: Weight-based volume and rate per maintenance/replacement calculations

admin: Administer by intravenous infusion only, with the rate and volume individualized to the patient
Use an infusion pump and monitor acid-base balance and electrolytes during therapy
Inspect solution for clarity and the container for integrity before use; do not use if cloudy or leaking
Avoid rapid infusion of hypertonic/molar sodium lactate; titrate to clinical and laboratory response
moa: Lactate ion is taken up by the liver (and to some extent other tissues) and metabolized through gluconeogenesis/oxidation, consuming hydrogen ions and generating bicarbonate. This raises plasma bicarbonate and pH, correcting metabolic acidosis. The accompanying sodium contributes to extracellular fluid volume and electrolyte balance.

absolute: Lactic acidosis (cannot use lactate as a bicarbonate source)
Severe hepatic impairment with impaired lactate metabolism
Conditions where added sodium is harmful (severe fluid overload, decompensated heart failure)
relative: Renal impairment / oliguria (fluid, sodium, potassium accumulation)
monitor: Fluid balance and signs of overload

preg: Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann's) is widely used in pregnancy and the peripartum period and is considered acceptable when an isotonic alkalinizing crystalloid is indicated; monitor fluid and electrolyte status.
lact: Considered compatible with breastfeeding; sodium and lactate are normal physiological constituents.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment. Reduced excretion increases the risk of fluid overload, hypernatremia, and (with compound solutions) hyperkalemia. Lactate clearance may also be impaired. Monitor electrolytes and fluid status closely.
hepatic: Use with caution and avoid in severe hepatic impairment, because the liver is required to convert lactate to bicarbonate; in hepatic failure lactate may accumulate and worsen acidosis rather than correct it.

major: Potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs (with potassium-containing compound solutions - hyperkalemia)
moderate: Corticosteroids / corticotropin (additive sodium and fluid retention)
Digoxin (caution with the calcium content of compound sodium lactate)
Ceftriaxone (incompatibility with calcium-containing solutions such as Hartmann's, especially in neonates)
minor: Lithium (sodium load can increase renal lithium clearance, lowering levels)
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant to acute IV use
interactions.diagnostics: Raises plasma bicarbonate and pH; alters serum sodium and lactate measurements

common: Fluid retention / edema with excess volume
serious: Hypernatremia and fluid overload / pulmonary edema
rare: Worsening lactic acidosis in hepatic failure or shock
emergency: Severe electrolyte or acid-base disturbance with arrhythmia or seizures

monitoring: Fluid balance, body weight, and signs of overload
Blood glucose (compound solutions may affect it; lactate is a gluconeogenic substrate)
counsel: This fluid is given as a drip in hospital to balance your salts and acid levels
Tell staff if you have heart, kidney, or liver problems
Report breathlessness, swelling, or palpitations during the infusion
Your blood salts and acid balance will be checked during treatment
pk: Alkalinizing effect develops as lactate is metabolized to bicarbonate (over ~1-2 hours)
Plasma bicarbonate rises during and shortly after the infusion
Lactate is rapidly metabolized by a healthy liver; clearance is delayed in hepatic dysfunction/shock
Effect persists while infusion continues; titrate to acid-base goals
Store at room temperature; protect from freezing; inspect for clarity before use; single-use containers
pearls: Lactate is an indirect (delayed) bicarbonate source - it must be metabolized by the liver, so it is ineffective and potentially harmful in hepatic failure or established lactic acidosis
Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann's/lactated Ringer's) uses lactate as its buffer - the basis of 'balanced' resuscitation fluids
Avoid co-infusion with ceftriaxone owing to calcium-ceftriaxone precipitation (notably in neonates)
Regional EMA/SmPC/BNF product - dosing is individualized; not a single US FDA oral monograph
missed: Not applicable - sodium lactate is an intravenous fluid titrated by clinicians to acid-base and fluid status, not a self-administered scheduled medication.
overdose: Excess produces metabolic alkalosis, hypernatremia, fluid overload, and electrolyte disturbance (and, in hepatic failure, lactate accumulation). Management: stop the infusion, treat fluid overload (diuretics, fluid restriction), correct electrolytes and acid-base disturbance, and provide supportive care.
